newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kia faces difficulties on all fronts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kia faces difficulties on all fronts.

text.p: The troubles of South Korea's beleaguered Kia Group were expected to worsen this week as more of its subcontractors face default, bankers baulk at discounting its bills and creditors press for its top executives to step down.
But the nation's eighth largest conglomerate, having rejected creditors' demands, insisted it would survive.
The Dong-A Ilbo newspaper said on Sunday flagship Kia Motors and some vendors were due to pay 180 billion won ($201.6 million) worth of promissory notes this week.
The daily said other domestic carmakers which had not stockpiled car components could be forced to halt production.
So far few of Kia's 5,000 subcontractors have defaulted on their debts but most are suffering from financial problems.

"The financial constraints of subcontractors are really serious as Kia's promissory notes kept by vendors are not being properly discounted," said a director of Kia Group who asked not to be identified.
"Kia is in good shape and we are quite sure of normalising our business, as long as creditors keep their credit lines open to us as they did before," he said.
The director said Kia had provided financial supports to its vendors, but analysts questioned how long the struggling group could help.
Kim So-rim, general manager of Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association, said nearly half of Kia's vendors also supplied parts to other carmakers.
"Kia might have some ammunition to fire, but I'm wondering how much and how long they can help," Kim said. "Without government help, it looks very difficult."
Kia Motors raised an estimated 350 billion won in cash in July by selling passenger and commercial vehicles at a 29.9 percent discount.
Analysts said Kia had no choice but to sell its products at a discount to generate fresh hard currency, but they said they worried about Kia Motors' deteriorating profitability.
In order to boost domestic sales, Kia Motors introduced updated versions of its Credos sedan and Sephia sub-compact in the past two weeks at prices of its old models.
But banks have refused to finance Kia's instalment sales, forcing the carmaker to turn to financial factoring firms, which would mean higher interest costs for buyers, Kia said.
Kia's car exports have remained solid. Kia shipped 31,990 vehicles in July, up from 22,964 a year earlier.

However, brisk overseas sales might not translate into good cash flow as banks have hesitated to deal with Kia's export bills and to respect Kia's letters of credit, said an official at Korea First Bank, Kia's major creditor.
"Especially foreign banks operating in Korea have stopped discounting Kia's export bills," said Ahn Jae-wook, operation manager at National Australia Bank.
"If a company is put under protection by the bail-out committee, foreign banks view the company as having defaulted."
Creditors in July put Kia Group under protection after they determined that Kia affiliates were on the verge of defaulting. The protection has been extended until September 29.
They also agreed to provide emergency loans of 183.1 billion won, but only if top Kia executives including group chairman Kim Sun-hong tendered resignation letters. The group has refused.

"Who else can better help Kia survive than the current management? Do you change captains when war breaks out?," the Kia director said. "We think creditors might have another intention rather than normalising our business."
There have been suggestions that creditor banks have taken a hard stand towards Kia because they would like to force a third-party takeover of Kia Motors.
